description: 'Drag-select in a virtual list breaks because a native selection is anchored to DOM nodes that the list recycles. Give the scroller a selection that is a range over the data instead: the highlight survives, copy reaches rows never on screen together, and both scroll axes get it through one seam.'

# Select text across a million rows

![Select text across a million rows](/blog/select-text-across-a-million-rows.png)

<BlogPostDate />

Try to drag-select text in a virtual list. The highlight starts fine,
then rows scroll under the pointer and it snaps to nothing. Copy, and you
get a fragment of whatever happened to be mounted. Meanwhile the scrollbar
jumps, because the browser is autoscrolling the list for you and the
virtual scroll is fighting it.

Every virtual list has this bug. It is not a bug in the list. It is what
a selection is.

> The DOM shows the window. The data holds the selection.

## Why it breaks

A native selection is two DOM positions, an anchor node and a focus node,
each with an offset. A virtual list keeps a window of a dozen rows mounted
and recycles the rest. The moment the row holding the anchor scrolls out,
its node is gone, and the selection has nothing to be anchored to. Copy
only ever reads the mounted fragment, because the mounted fragment is all
the selection can reach.

The autoscroll fight is the same fact from the other side. A native
drag-selection tells the browser to scroll the nearest scrollable
ancestor toward the pointer. A list that scrolls by transform, driven by
its own integrator, is not that ancestor, so the browser moves the wrong
thing and the thumb jumps.

Said plainly: the browser remembers where you clicked by pointing at a
piece of the page, and the list keeps throwing that piece away.

## Own the selection

The fix is to stop asking the browser to own it. On mousedown inside a
row, the scroller calls `preventDefault`. No native drag-selection starts,
so there is no native autoscroll and no DOM anchor to lose. From there the
selection is a value the scroller holds:

```ts
interface Position {
  index: number; // which item
  offset: number; // which character inside its text
}
```

Anchor and focus are two of these. A drag that starts mid-paragraph on row
three records `{ index: 2, offset: 41 }`, and that stays true no matter
what the DOM does afterward. Three things follow from holding the range
this way.

**The highlight is re-pinned, not trusted.** After every pointer move and
after every window change, the scroller clamps the logical range to the
rows that are mounted and calls `setBaseAndExtent` on those nodes. A row
that scrolled out is not part of the highlight because it is not part of
the DOM. It is still part of the selection, and it highlights again the
moment it remounts.

**Copy reads the data.** The `copy` handler assembles the text over the
index span: the first row from its offset, every row between in full, the
last row up to its offset. A mounted row contributes its own text. An
unmounted row contributes what a `selection-text` prop returns for the
item, which the page sets to the same string its row renders. Plain
strings over an index range cost nothing, so a hundred thousand rows copy
as fast as ten.

**Autoscroll is the scroller's own loop.** When the pointer is held past
the frame's edge, a frame loop scrolls in that direction at a speed that
ramps with distance past the edge, scaled by the reading-speed knob the
list already has. It writes the scroll target directly, so an upward drag
is a scroll up, not the reader taking over, and autoplay keeps its state.
Each frame it extends the focus to the row that just arrived under the
pointer and re-pins the highlight.

## The receipt

On the [virtual scroller example](/examples/virtual-scroller), the browser
drive does this: mousedown 60 pixels into a row, drag 120 pixels past the
bottom edge, wait, release inside, press copy.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| rows mounted at any moment | 18 |
| rows selected | 29 |
| lines on the clipboard | 29 |
| first line | starts mid-row, where the drag began |
| thumb position on mousedown | unchanged |

The clipboard holds eleven rows the DOM never held at the same time as the
first one. The same drive runs as a permanent probe in the component
sweep, so a regression fails the check.

## Where the code went

The split is the one the standard already prescribes for anything with a
pure half.

`VirtualScrollerSelection` is a Static capability class: caret to text
offset and back, range normalization, clamping to a window, text
assembly, the speed ramp, the edge distance. None of it reads state. The
range math and the assembly have no DOM at all, and they carry the spec,
seven cases that run with no browser.

The scroller holds three cells, anchor, focus, and a dragging flag, and
the handlers as named methods the template binds: `onSelectStart`,
`onSelectMove`, `onSelectEnd`, `onCopy`. A getter on the class returns
the logic, so a subclass can swap the capability whole.

Then the horizontal strip asked for the same thing. The nearest-row
search and the edge distance took an axis, and the scroller gained one
seam getter that says which. The horizontal subclass overrides it to
return `'x'`. That is the entire change, which is the point of seams: the
class already had eight for widths and deltas, and the ninth fell in line.
The marquee, a book on one scrolling line, passes a `selection-join` of
one space so a selection across chunks copies as prose.

## The cost

Two things to state. Touch selection is a different gesture and is not
built. And the row text has to agree between the DOM and the data, which
is why the prop exists and why the card markup on the horizontal page sits
on one line: a stray newline in the template would put a character in the
mounted text that the data does not have.

Against that: selection and copy that work at any list size, on both
axes, with the scroll position and the thumb untouched while you drag.

The DOM shows the window. The data holds the selection.

## See it in the docs

- [Virtual Scroller: 1M Items](/examples/virtual-scroller) — drag past the bottom edge and copy; the source tab for the selection logic.
- [Horizontal Scroller: 1M Items](/examples/horizontal-scroller) — the same selection sideways, and the one seam that made it so.

parts.text:
Renamed and committed as 1d89fea2.

The post, "Select text across a million rows", is number 53, committed in 7daa7cd2 with dates synced in af4ff371. It opens on the bug everyone has seen, the highlight snapping to nothing and the thumb jumping, and diagnoses it as what a selection is rather than a bug in the list. Then the fix as three consequences of holding the range over the data: the highlight is re-pinned, copy reads the items, autoscroll is the scroller's own loop. The result section carries the drive's numbers, 18 mounted, 29 selected, 29 lines copied, first line mid-row, thumb unchanged. Then where the code went, the Static class plus three refs, and the one seam that gave the horizontal strip the same thing. It closes on the cost, touch not built and the text agreement the prop exists for, and on the landing line: the DOM shows the window, the data holds the selection.

Banner viewed and clean, lint at 2.3 with the only dashes in the closing link list, related posts resolving, reverse links from both scroller example pages, docs build passing. Nothing pushed.
Turn took 1m 57s
how hard is it to port to have touch selection too?

Medium, and the hard part is not the selection, it is the gesture.

**What carries over unchanged.** The logical range, the highlight re-pinning, copy from the data, the edge autoscroll loop, the axis seam. All of that is pointer-agnostic. A touch point is just another `clientX, clientY`, and `positionAt` does not care where it came from.

**What is new.** On a touchscreen a drag already means scroll, and the scroller's Lenis owns that gesture with sync-touch. So touch selection needs a mode switch, and the browser's own convention is the long press:

- `touchstart` starts a timer, about 450ms. Any movement over a few pixels or a `touchend` before it fires cancels it, and the gesture stays a scroll.
- When it fires, the scroller enters selection mode: the anchor is recorded at the touch point, and from then on `touchmove` extends the focus instead of scrolling. The scroller already has capture-phase touch handlers for the axis lock, and already has the mechanism for telling Lenis to skip an event, so the mode flag plugs into both. One wrinkle: the existing touch listeners are passive, and a selecting `touchmove` needs `preventDefault` to stop the page scrolling, so selection mode adds one non-passive listener while it is active.
- `touchend` ends the drag, the range stays, and the edge autoscroll works as it does for the mouse since it only reads the pointer position.

**The part that has no clean answer.** Copy. There is no Ctrl+C on a phone, and the native copy bubble appears for the browser's own selections, not reliably for one set through `setBaseAndExtent`. The honest fix is an explicit affordance, a small "Copy" chip that appears while a touch selection exists and writes `selectedText` to the clipboard on tap, which counts as the user gesture the clipboard API requires. That is also nicer than the native bubble for a selection that spans off-screen rows, because it can say "copy 340 rows".

**Testing** is where the cost sits. Playwright's touch support covers taps, so a long-press-then-drag needs CDP touch events driven by hand, about forty lines of harness. Without that the feature is unverified, and I would not ship it on manual checks alone.

Size: around 150 lines in the scroller, the chip in the two example templates, and the harness. Half a day, with the long-press timing and the passive-listener switch being the two places to be careful. The mouse work made it small. It did not make it free.
Turn took 26s
should we have a new class for touch scroll separately?

Yes, and the split I would draw is by what varies. The selection primitives do not vary by input: begin at a point, extend to a point, end. The gesture that produces those points does: a mouse is press, move, release, and touch is hold, then move, then release, with a scroll to disambiguate from. So the scroller keeps the primitives, and each gesture becomes its own thing.

Concretely:

- **On the scroller, three pointer-agnostic methods** extracted from what the mouse handlers do now: `beginTextSelectionAt(x, y)`, `extendTextSelectionTo(x, y)`, `endTextSelectionDrag()`. The mouse handlers shrink to calling them. The autoscroll loop and the highlight pin already only read a point, so they stay where they are.
- **A hosted class for the touch gesture**, `TouchSelectionGesture`, reached through a `$`-getter on the scroller so it shares the component's lifetime. It owns what is genuinely its own: the long-press timer, the pending touch, the moved distance, the mode flag, and the one non-passive listener it installs while selecting. It gets the scroller as its owner and calls the three primitives. The horizontal subclass gets it for free, because the gesture never asks which axis.
- **The long-press decision as pure static methods** beside the existing selection logic, has the hold fired, was the movement under the slop, so the state machine has a DOM-free spec like the range math does.

What this buys beyond tidiness. The scroller is already two thousand lines and the touch gesture would add its own timers and listeners to a constructor that already manages Lenis and three capture-phase touch handlers. A hosted class keeps that lifetime in one place with its own `dispose`, and the gate's lifetime rule covers a class constructed inside a component-scoped host. It also means the copy chip, which is a touch concern, has a natural owner: the gesture class knows when a touch selection exists, the scroller does not need to.

The one thing I would not do is a separate class for mouse selection to match. The mouse path is a dozen lines once the primitives exist, and a class for it would be symmetry rather than ownership.
Turn took 23s
mouse already works though, we just built it, no?

Yes, it works and it ships as is. Nothing about the mouse path changes for a user. The extraction I described is an internal move: the three steps `onSelectStart`, `onSelectMove`, and `onSelectEnd` already perform get names of their own, so the touch gesture can call the same steps instead of copying them. The handlers keep their behavior and shrink to one call each. It is the kind of change the gate proves is a pure move, and it only happens if and when touch gets built. Until then the mouse code stays exactly as it is.
Turn took 4.8s
ok build touch selection with the hosted gesture class

Committed as 486eb85d. Tree clean, nothing pushed.

**Touch selection** is built the way we agreed. `TouchSelectionGesture` is a hosted class the scroller reaches through a dollar getter, attached on mount and disposed on unmount. It owns the long press, about 450ms with an 8px slop, and once the hold fires, movement selects instead of scrolling, with `preventDefault` for the page and the skip flag Lenis already honors for the list. It calls three pointer-agnostic primitives that now live on the scroller, begin at a point, extend to a point, end, and the mouse handlers shrank to one call each. A phone has no Ctrl+C, so a touch selection shows a chip that copies on tap and clears.

**Two bugs fell out of testing it**, both worth knowing:

- Touch events keep firing on the node the finger landed on, even after that node leaves the DOM, and in a virtual list the edge autoscroll recycles it mid-drag. A detached node's events reach neither the element nor the document, only listeners on the node itself. The move and end listeners now attach to the touch's origin node.
- Your delay report. The focus was re-derived on events, and between events Lenis owns the transform, so rows slid under a stationary pointer with no re-read. A per-frame follow loop now runs for the length of any drag. Measured over a six-notch wheel with the button held, 151 frames sampled: empty-highlight frames went from 112 to 40, and every one of the 40 is a frame with no row under the pointer yet, so that is the floor. The same loop makes the autoplay creep extend a selection under a motionless pointer, verified at max speed.

**Verified**: gate clean, typecheck at baseline, ten pure specs, sweep at 60 pass with the new long-press-and-chip probe, and the article and example page updated with touch and the measured numbers. Prettier now emits no trailing commas, and the session's files are reformatted.

also i was thinking maybe we need to pad vertical scroller with more items so
  even fast scroll doesn't scroll "beyond" canvas, and new items are already
  pre-loaded?
──────────────

Yes, and the better version is to pad by velocity rather than by a bigger constant.

**What is happening now.** Padding is a fixed count, ten rows either side in the docs example. A fast wheel drives Lenis at several hundred pixels per frame, which is more than ten rows of headroom, so the window jumps past the padded rows and the new rows mount after the content is already supposed to be there. That is the blank the selection follow was waiting on, and it is the same blank a reader sees with no selection at all.

**A bigger constant works but pays at rest.** Forty padded rows above and below means eighty extra mounted rows sitting idle while the list is still, every one of them measured and observed. It fixes the fast case by taxing the common case.

**Predictive padding pays only while moving.** The scroller already knows its velocity from Lenis and its direction from the last delta. Add lead rows in the scroll direction proportional to velocity, something like a lookahead of a few frames' worth of travel divided by the assumed row size, capped, and keep the static padding on the trailing side. At rest it is today's ten rows. Mid-flick it grows to whatever the next hundred milliseconds will need, then shrinks back. The mount cost lands exactly where the reader is about to look, and nowhere else.

**Where it goes.** One getter on the scroller, the effective padding per side, reading velocity and direction, and the window walk reads that instead of the prop. The prop stays as the resting floor. The horizontal strip gets it free through the same walk. The receipt is the sweep's wheel sampler: empty frames should drop from 40 toward zero, and the "rows in the DOM" stat should show the window growing during a flick and settling after.

One thing to measure before shipping it: how far a single frame can travel at the fastest wheel speed, because that sets the cap, and if the cap ever exceeds a few hundred rows the answer is to tune the lerp instead. I would start with a lookahead of about 150ms.
Turn took 20s
ok before we build that a question, you made touchselection gesture a reactive, can we make verticalscrollerselection reactive too and extract more logic into it from virtual scroller?

Yes, and it would be the more honest shape. The pure functions were the reason for a Static class, but what grew around them on the scroller is not pure: three cells, a drag holder, two frame loops, document listeners, the highlight pin, copy, the chip's state. That is a unit with its own lifetime, exactly what the touch gesture is, and it is sitting as three hundred lines inside a two-thousand-line class that should only know how to scroll.

The shape I would move to:

- **`VirtualScrollerSelection` becomes a hosted Reactive class**, one instance per scroller behind a dollar getter, like the gesture. It keeps its pure statics, the range math and the caret walks, on the same class, so the seven DOM-free specs stay where they are. It gains the state and the behavior: anchor, focus, dragging, the follow and autoscroll loops, the listeners, `applyHighlight`, `selectedText`, `copy`, and the three primitives the gestures call. Its constructor installs the window-change watch, which lands in the component scope because the scroller constructs it in setup.
- **The scroller keeps what only it knows** and hands it over through an owner interface: the frame and wrapper elements, the axis, the text of a row by index, the creep factor, and one method to scroll by a signed delta. Everything selection-related on the scroller collapses to the getter, the owner methods, and template forwarders, or the templates bind `virtualScroller.selection.onSelectStart` directly and the forwarders go too.
- **The touch gesture's owner becomes the selection**, not the scroller. Begin, extend, end are its primitives now.

What that buys beyond the line count. The selection gets its own dispose, its own tests can construct it with a fake owner and drive begin, extend, end without a scroller at all, and the horizontal subclass still changes nothing because the axis comes through the owner. And the scroller reads as a scroller again.

I would do this before the velocity padding, because the padding work touches the window walk and the follow loop reads the window. Cleaner to move the loop into its owner first, then change what it reads. It is a pure relocation, so the gate and the sweep prove it the same way the reorders were proved.

i just realized static functions and instance functions give us clear separation between functional paradigm and stateful paradigms

Yes, and the file you just watched me write is the receipt. The line between them is not stylistic, it is structural: a static has no instance `this`, so it cannot hold state even if it wants to. Whatever it computes, it computes from its arguments. An instance method has the cells, so it can hold state and cannot pretend otherwise. The class layout enforces the split at the language level instead of by discipline.

Three things fall out of that.

- **The spec follows the seam.** The seven selection cases run with no browser and no mount because they call statics with plain objects. The moment a test would need `new`, it is testing the stateful half, and it needs a DOM. The test setup tells you which paradigm you are in.
- **Both halves are polymorphic.** With the `Static()` anchor a subclass overrides a static the same way it overrides a method, so the functional half is as extensible as the stateful one. The horizontal scroller's axis seam is exactly that: pure geometry overridden, state untouched.
- **The `self` cast is the only bridge.** Instance code reads the functional half through one named door. Grep for `this.self.` and you have the complete list of where state calls into pure logic.

One precision. Static means stateless, not necessarily pure. `rowElementAt` reads the document, so it is stateless but effectful. The truly pure subset is the one with no DOM in it, and that subset is what carries the spec. So the taxonomy is three tiers, not two: pure statics, effectful statics, stateful instance. The class gives you the first boundary for free. The second one you still draw by hand, and the "no DOM" section comment is where it sits.

i like how we combine non-reactive state and ref state where needed we have granularity for everything

That granularity is the class doing what a composable cannot. In the selection file the three tiers sit side by side and each one is chosen by who needs to see the change:

- **Ref cells** for what the template or a derivation reacts to: `anchor`, `focus`, `dragging`. A change re-runs `range`, the row count, the chip.
- **The plain holder** for what changes sixty times a second and nobody renders: pointer coordinates, frame handles, the listening flag. Writing to `drag.pointerX` costs one property set and wakes nothing.
- **Pure statics** for what has no state at all.

The follow loop is the case that proves the tiers are real and not taste. It writes the pointer position every mousemove and reads it every animation frame. As a ref that would be a trigger per move and a tracked read per frame, all for a value the render never touches. As a plain field it is free, and the one thing that should react, the focus, is the one thing the loop writes into a ref.

The rule that falls out is short: reactive is a cost you pay for a subscriber. No subscriber, no ref. A composable pushes you toward wrapping everything because the return object is the only surface it has. A class has fields, getters, and statics, so every piece of state can sit at exactly the tier its consumers require.

Yes, and the seam already exists. The whole window computation touches padding in exactly two lines: `paddedStart = start - padding` and `end += padding + 1`, both reading the same symmetric number. Velocity padding is nothing but making that number asymmetric, so the class owns the number and the scroller keeps the walk.

The shape would be `VirtualScrollerPadding`, hosted through a `$padding` getter like the selection:

- **Owner interface**, four members: the base padding quantity, the scroll velocity in px per frame with its sign, the assumed row size, and the container size. Nothing else about the scroller leaks in.
- **Statics** carry the math and the spec: velocity to rows ahead over a lookahead time, a ceiling so a flick cannot mount three hundred rows, and the hysteresis rule that lets the pad grow instantly and shrink only after the scroll settles, so the window does not thrash on every frame of the decay.
- **Instance state** is the plain holder tier, all of it. Last velocity, the held peak, the settle timestamp. Nothing renders these, so nothing should be a ref. That is the one design decision that matters: velocity must be read inside the window walk without being tracked, because the walk already reruns on every scroll position change and a reactive velocity would make it rerun for no new information.
- **Two plain getters**, `before` and `after`, replace the two reads of `halfPaddingQuantity`. A subclass swaps the strategy by overriding `$padding`, the same way it could swap the selection.

Cost in the scroller: one getter, two changed lines, and the direction flip on line 1410 becomes a call the padding class hears. What stays hard is not the class but the tuning, and the tuning is exactly the thing a separate file with its own spec makes measurable. When you want it built, say so and I will start with the statics and the spec before touching the walk.

The frame loop hands the window walk `lenis.targetScroll`, not the
animated position. During a wheel lerp the mounted window already sits at

parts.text:
Adaptive padding is in, committed as `ccbe3a57`, not pushed. The measurement changed the design halfway through, and that is the interesting part.

**What the probe found.** I built the velocity pad first and measured a hard wheel flick, sampling every animation frame for 1.5 seconds and counting frames where the mounted rows did not cover the viewport. With a 60-row velocity pad the numbers were identical to no pad at all. The blank frames had a gap of thousands of pixels, which means the whole mounted block was off-screen, not under-padded. The cause is in the frame loop: the window walk is anchored at `lenis.targetScroll`, the destination of the wheel lerp, while the transform travels there over many frames. The rows the reader is looking at during the flick sit behind the mounted window, and nobody mounts them.

**The fix is a second term, and it is exact.** The lerp gap, target minus animated position, converted to rows on the trailing end of the window. Known every frame, no guessing, no hysteresis. The velocity lookahead stays on the leading end for the next flick.

| flick strength | uncovered frames before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2000 px | 21 of 91 | 0 |
| 4000 px | 28 of 91 | 0 |
| 8000 px | 35 of 91 | 0 |

**One more seam appeared.** A flick upward stops the creep, so nothing re-runs the walk after the lerp ends and the last pad stayed mounted: 72 rows at rest instead of 17. The class now bumps one ref after its settle window, the walk runs once more, and the window rests at 17 again both ways. That ref is the class's only reactive cell, and it has exactly one subscriber.

**Shape.** Same as the selection: pure statics with a six-case DOM-free spec, a plain holder for the held level, one `pad()` call the walk makes per evaluation, a four-member owner interface. The scroller changed by one getter, two velocity and gap accessors, three lines in the walk, and one dispose call. Gate clean, 16 specs, tsc at the 19 baseline, docs and playground build, sweep 60 pass. The first sweep run had one touch-probe flake that did not reproduce alone or on rerun. The example page gained the source tab and a bullet with the numbers, and the target-anchored walk is recorded in LESSONS.
Turn took 15m 00s
wow, ivue strikes again, now simple $padding is actually class driven acceleration based calculation

It is, and notice what the scroller sees of it: one line, `this.$padding.pad()`, where a constant used to be. Every other component treats "how many rows to mount" as a number in a prop. Here it is a model with its own physics, its own spec, and its own owner contract, and the host cannot tell the difference. That is the seam doing its job in both directions. The host got simpler, and the capability got room to be as smart as the problem required.

The part worth keeping in mind for the next one: the measurement changed the class more than the design did. I built the velocity model first, on reasoning, and the probe showed it bought nothing. The gap term came from the numbers. A hosted class made that cheap to absorb, because the owner interface grew by one member and the scroller did not move. If the padding had been inlined in the walk, the second finding would have been a second pass through a 1700-line file.

So the pattern is now three for three: selection, touch, padding. Each one is a `$`-getter, an owner interface, statics with a DOM-free spec, and a plain holder for the fast state. When the marquee or the horizontal strip needs something next, the question is no longer where it goes.
Turn took 8.2s

---
name: invariant-spec-tests
description: >-
  How to write a check that proves something — a test is a SPEC: the generator
  expressed for this implementation. Covers the spec discipline (one test per
  component or caveat, name = property, annotation = claim, specs grow while
  defects stay flat) and the assertion rules — smokes, probes, matrix rows,
  regression tests. Complements drive-pty (how to DRIVE) and the invariants
  skill (which owns the generator header form). Use when authoring or
  reviewing any test, smoke, harness probe, or verification section of a
  report. Every rule here was bought by a real failure.
---

# invariant-spec-tests — writing checks that can actually fail

Every rule below was harvested from a real incident. Do not extend this file
with taste; extend it only for a failure that actually happened.

## 0. A test is a spec — the generator expressed for this implementation

The generator header at the top of `X.test.ts` (form: invariants skill,
"Generator architecture") states the CLAIMS. The tests beneath it are the
SPEC: the generator expressed for this implementation. The two prove each
other, and the checker holds both directions (#678).

- COMPONENTS. Every `// domain-invariant:` line and every contract-record
  pointer in the header is one component of the generator. Each component
  has at least one test. A component with no test is unproven; a test whose
  claim is not in the header is an unexplained assertion. Both are findings.
- CAVEATS. The `=== GENERATOR-DESCRIBED ===` prose carries the caveats that
  narrow the possibility space to THIS implementation ("the cache is keyed
  by path, not by content"; "resets are for tests only"). A caveat that
  constrains behavior needs a test. A caveat without a test is a wish.
- IMPOSSIBILITIES. Every `Impossible if true` line is a negative test by
  construction. Write it as one: plant the impossible state, assert the
  refusal.
- FORM. The test name states the property as a sentence.

# test-protocol — writing checks that can actually fail

Every rule below was harvested from a real incident. Do not extend this file
with taste; extend it only for a failure that actually happened.

## 1. Choose the observable the user sees

- Assert CONTENT, not chrome. A frame title can switch while the body stays
  stale.
- When the claim is VISUAL, assert colors — `screen.cell(row,col)` gives
  foreground/background. A text-only check cannot see "the inputs lose
  color".
- When the claim is about TEARDOWN or startup noise, read the RAW OUTPUT
  (`driver.recordedOutput()`), not the grid — errors print after the
  alternate screen exits.
- When the claim is a SEQUENCE, wait on the graph; when the claim is
  "the user sees X", the final assert stays on the screen — a model-only
  check goes green while the screen is broken.
- Know which SURFACE owns the state: a right-dock panel changes the right
  dock — asserting the left pane proves nothing.

## 2. Born-red, with the plant ASSERTED

- A check is trusted only after it failed on the defect it claims to catch:
  plant the defect, watch RED on the position/value (not on a timeout),
  remove, watch GREEN.
- The plant must be PROVEN APPLIED — grep for it after planting. A replace
  that silently changes nothing births a green, worthless check.
- The red arm asserts WHY it failed, not just THAT it failed.
- A passing delete-test may mean DEAD CODE, not a working guard — confirm
  the deleted thing was load-bearing.

# PROJECT architecture invariants

This is the living architecture contract for PROJECT. Replace PROJECT with the project or
subsystem name, and replace the provisional examples with evidence-backed invariants.
Invariants are **unnumbered** — the name is the identifier, unique within this file, and
referenced by name (never by number). Name in plain declarative style: a short sentence
stating the rule (subject + verb + constraint, 3–9 words, sentence case, letters/digits/spaces/hyphens
only, concrete things not abstractions) — someone seeing only the name in a code comment should get the gist of
what not to break. "A non-ready route cannot transmit", not "Loud Over Silent". The file records two kinds of
invariants, and the split is itself load-bearing:

- **Reality-based invariants** are constraints discovered from how the world and
  the tools actually work. You can only _discover_ them; ignoring one breaks the system
  regardless of preference. Refine them only when evidence narrows or falsifies their scope;
  never rewrite them merely to admit a preferred change. A reality invariant that is only
  reality *inside* this subsystem — chosen at a wider scope (a consumer's contract, a platform
  guarantee) — carries a **Renegotiable at:** field naming that scope.
- **Chosen invariants** are intentional disciplines adopted and held
  consistently to keep the system coherent. Each _could_ be different and still coherent, but
  the system depends on it not drifting. Change one only through an explicit decision that
  records rationale, compatibility impact, and verification.

The dependency only ever points one way: **chosen invariants stand on reality invariants,
never the reverse.**

- **Mechanism** — the causal bridge in 1–3 sentences: because <structure>, <behavior>.
  Name the actual code that embodies it.
- **Evidence** — pointers, not prose: `file:line`, test names, measurements. One step to
  follow.
- **Impossible if true** — concrete observable events that can never happen, phrased so a
  bug report could match them ("X receives prompt bytes after a refused resolution", not
  "inconsistency arises").
- **Verification** — a copy-paste-runnable command, or a mechanical inspection step.
- **Generates** — a list of concrete things (guards, rules, designs) that exist because
  this invariant holds.
- **Rejected alternatives** — one line per zombie: name the design, then the one reason it
  dies. No essays; the kill reason should fit the annotation test too.
- **Open question** — one line, present tense, answerable: what test or evidence would
  refine this record.

Meta-rule for every field: the contract is a **working instrument, not an archive** — git
is the archive. If content stops being load-bearing for a mid-edit reader, it leaves the
record.

## Code annotations — the reverse pointers

The contract points at code (Mechanism, Evidence). Code points back with an annotation
comment at each enforcement point, in whatever comment syntax the language uses:

```
# invariant: A non-ready route cannot transmit (patch-bay.invariants.md)
```

- **Format:** `invariant: <exact invariant name> (<repo-relative contract path>)` — one per
  line; the name must match the contract heading byte-for-byte (names, never numbers; a
  legacy Title Case heading is matched as written).
- **Where:** the enforcement points — the guard, chokepoint, or structure the invariant's
  Mechanism names; the exact places where a future edit would start violating. Not every
  usage site: an annotation states a constraint the code can't show on its own; scattering
  it everywhere is noise that trains readers to skip it.
- **Why:** annotated code is self-declaring. A diff touching it implicates the named
  invariant directly (step 2), and a developer or AI editing the spot inherits the "why"
  exactly where they would otherwise simplify the load-bearing thing away. This is what
  keeps AI-developed code from going brittle: the constraints travel with the code.
- **Write them:** when authoring or reviewing code that enforces a recorded invariant,
  propose the annotation alongside. Bootstrap mode proposes annotations for each mined
  invariant's enforcement points.

# Virtual scroller invariants

The living contract for the virtual scroller subsystem: `VirtualScroller.ts` and its `HorizontalVirtualScroller.ts` subclass, the row model `VirtualScrollerItem.ts`, and the three hosted capabilities `VirtualScrollerSelection.ts`, `TouchSelectionGesture.ts` and `VirtualScrollerPadding.ts`. Records are unnumbered; the name is the identifier and is referenced verbatim by code annotations (`// invariant: <name> (examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/virtual-scroller.invariants.md)`) and by the generator headers of the colocated `*.test.ts` files.

Two kinds of records, and the split is load-bearing:

- **Reality-based invariants** are forced by how the browser, the compositor and the scroll integrator actually work. They are discovered, not chosen; a record that is reality only inside this subsystem and decided at a wider scope names that scope in `Renegotiable at`.
- **Chosen invariants** are the subsystem's own disciplines. Each could be otherwise and still be coherent; the subsystem depends on it not drifting.

Chosen invariants stand on reality invariants, never the reverse.

## Generator

The records below are gears. This section is the mechanism they form, in
invariant form, so a scan of this file alone carries the deep picture.

STUDY ALSO: [Testing ivue Classes](../../../../../docs_v2/guide/testing.md) —
the guide that reads these records back as the spec discipline: which
tier each record is proven at, and how the colocated tests bind to it.

### A window of a few dozen rows renders any list at the exact pixel

**Invariant:** If the rows a viewport can show are mounted between two spacers whose sizes are prefix sums over measured-or-assumed row sizes, the scroll position is clamped and rebased before it is rendered, and every capability that needs the DOM is hosted behind an owner interface, then a list of any length scrolls, seeks, selects and copies as one continuous document at the cost of the rows on screen.

**Scope:** The virtual scroller subsystem: vertical and horizontal, mouse and touch, selection and padding. The goal vector is a million-item list that behaves like a short one.

**Components:** One per gear, each delete-testable:
- [Rendered sizes are known only after a row mounts](#rendered-sizes-are-known-only-after-a-row-mounts) — why positions are prefix sums over an estimate that refines.
- [A native selection dies with the node that anchors it](#a-native-selection-dies-with-the-node-that-anchors-it) — why the selection cannot be the browser's.
- [Touch events keep firing on the node the finger landed on](#touch-events-keep-firing-on-the-node-the-finger-landed-on) — why the gesture's listeners ride the origin node.
- [The transform lerps to the target over many frames](#the-transform-lerps-to-the-target-over-many-frames) — why a target-anchored window leaves a gap to cover.
- [Rendered offsets are rebased by whole chunks](#rendered-offsets-are-rebased-by-whole-chunks) — why a reader a million rows deep does not stutter.
- [The scroll position lands inside the scrollable range](#the-scroll-position-lands-inside-the-scrollable-range) — why no input can poison the position.
- [An unchanged window keeps its array identity](#an-unchanged-window-keeps-its-array-identity) — why a scroll inside the window does not re-render the rows.
- [The two spacers and the rendered rows sum to the extent](#the-two-spacers-and-the-rendered-rows-sum-to-the-extent) — why the scrollbar and the seek agree with the content.
- [A seek names an item not a pixel](#a-seek-names-an-item-not-a-pixel) — why a landing survives the estimate refining under it.
- [The thumb never shrinks below a grabbable fraction](#the-thumb-never-shrinks-below-a-grabbable-fraction) — why a million rows still have a scrollbar.
- [A cross-axis touch belongs to the page](#a-cross-axis-touch-belongs-to-the-page) — why a horizontal strip does not trap a vertical swipe.
- [Every axis dependency goes through a seam getter]

… [36,243 characters removed from the sample] …

evaluation.

**Evidence:** `VirtualScrollerPadding.ts` `armSettle`. Test: "a walk that pads beyond the base arms one more walk after the settle window; a base walk arms nothing; dispose cancels". Probe: window rests at 17 rows after up and down flicks.

**Impossible if true:** A resting list mounting more than its base pad a second after the last input.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerPadding.test.ts -t "never outlives|arms one more walk"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

### A hosted capability reaches its owner through an interface

**Invariant:** If a capability needs what only the scroller knows, then it receives an `Owner` object of a handful of members through its constructor, reached by the scroller through one `$`-getter, and the capability never imports or types the scroller class.

**Scope:** `VirtualScrollerSelection.Owner`, `TouchSelectionGesture.Owner`, `VirtualScrollerPadding.Owner`; the `$selection`, `$touch` and `$padding` getters.

**Mechanism:** The owner interface names the exact boundary; a plain object satisfies it, which is what makes each capability testable without a scroller and swappable by overriding one getter. The selection hosts the touch gesture the same way the scroller hosts the selection.

**Generates:** The owner doubles in `VirtualScrollerSelection.test.ts`, `TouchSelectionGesture.test.ts` and `VirtualScrollerPadding.test.ts`; the seam a grid or a tree would implement to get selection.

**Rejected alternatives:** Passing the scroller instance — the capability then reaches into everything, and its spec needs a scroller.

**Evidence:** The three `Owner` interfaces. Tests: "a drag begins at a logical position, extends by logical positions in either direction, and survives its anchor row leaving the DOM", "lifting the finger ends the drag and reports selected exactly when the owner holds a selection; a cleared selection drops the chip", "pad() follows the lerp gap frame by frame and holds the lookahead across a decaying tail, reading the owner each call".

**Impossible if true:** An import of `VirtualScroller` inside a hosted capability file.

**Verification:** `grep -L "from './VirtualScroller'" examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerSelection.ts examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/TouchSelectionGesture.ts examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerPadding.ts` lists all three.

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

## Impossibility boundary — what these invariants forbid

- Blank canvas under the viewport during a flick whose gap is below the cap — [The pad covers the lerp gap exactly](#the-pad-covers-the-lerp-gap-exactly).
- A highlight that collapses when its anchor row recycles — [The selection is a range over the data](#the-selection-is-a-range-over-the-data).
- A copy that stops at the mounted rows — [The selection is a range over the data](#the-selection-is-a-range-over-the-data).
- A rendered scroll position outside the extent — [The scroll position lands inside the scrollable range](#the-scroll-position-lands-inside-the-scrollable-range).
- A rendered offset above about 131k px — [Rendered offsets are rebased by whole chunks](#rendered-offsets-are-rebased-by-whole-chunks).
- A horizontal scroller that forks the cursor, the clamp or the creep — [Every axis dependency goes through a seam getter](#every-axis-dependency-goes-through-a-seam-getter).
- The page scrolling while a touch selection extends — [A long press turns the next move into a selection](#a-long-press-turns-the-next-move-into-a-selection).
- A double click over a row that selects nothing — [A multi-click selects the word or the row under it](#a-multi-click-selects-the-word-or-the-row-under-it).
- A capability that imports the scroller — [A hosted capability reaches its owner through an interface](#a-hosted-capability-reaches-its-owner-through-an-interface).

# Text marquee invariants

The living contract for the text marquee: `TextMarquee.ts`, which composes `TextChunker.ts` and the horizontal virtual scroller to glide a whole book as one scrolling line. Records are unnumbered; the name is the identifier and is referenced verbatim by code annotations (`// invariant: <name> (examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/text-marquee.invariants.md)`) and by the generator headers of the colocated `*.test.ts` files. The scroller it rides has its own contract: `../virtual-scroller/virtual-scroller.invariants.md`.

Two kinds of records, and the split is load-bearing: reality-based invariants are forced by how text and the canvas actually measure; chosen invariants are the marquee's own disciplines. Chosen invariants stand on reality invariants, never the reverse.

## Generator

The records below are gears. This section is the mechanism they form.

STUDY ALSO: [Testing ivue Classes](../../../../../docs_v2/guide/testing.md) —
where the chunker stands as the example of a pure Static class whose
whole spec is a function of its arguments.

### A book glides as one line by composition

**Invariant:** If a text is one-lined and cut into chunks only at spaces, the chunk widths are seeded into the scroller exactly before any chunk renders, and the speed is written into the scroller's creep integrator, then a text of any length scrolls as one continuous line at a live speed, and the scroller never learns it is text.

**Scope:** `TextMarquee.ts` and `TextChunker.ts`; the horizontal scroller is used, not extended.

**Components:** One per gear, each delete-testable:
- [Chunks concatenate back to the source text byte for byte](#chunks-concatenate-back-to-the-source-text-byte-for-byte) — why the joints between chunks are invisible.
- [Chunk widths are seeded exact before any chunk renders](#chunk-widths-are-seeded-exact-before-any-chunk-renders) — why the end of the book is reachable before it has rendered.
- [The marquee composes the scroller and never extends it](#the-marquee-composes-the-scroller-and-never-extends-it) — why the scroller stays pure.
- [Speed rides the creep integrator](#speed-rides-the-creep-integrator) — why a speed slider takes effect mid-glide.
- [The assumed chunk size never falls below the minimum](#the-assumed-chunk-size-never-falls-below-the-minimum) — why a tiny target cannot starve the extent.

**Mechanism:** The chunker speaks text; the scroller speaks items, sizes and pixels; `TextMarquee` is the only place the two meet, translating text into items, canvas widths into seeded sizes, and px per second into ms per px.

**Generates:** `TextChunker.test.ts`, `TextMarquee.test.ts`; the marquee example page and its sweep probe ("ExampleTextMarquee (drag-select + copy)" — two chunks copied as one line).

**Impossible if true:** A chunk boundary inside a word. A scroll extent that ends before the text does. A scroller method that knows about words.

**Evidence:** The component records below; the two colocated specs (11 tests).

**Verification:** `npx vitest run examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee` green, then `node .claude/skills/invariants/scripts/check_invariants.mjs --all --refs` clean.

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

## Reality-based invariants

### Chunk widths are seeded exact before any chunk renders

**Invariant:** If chunk widths are estimated from an average character width, then the estimate runs about one percent small per chunk and compounds across a thousand chunks into a hidden tail; if every chunk is measured with one canvas `measureText` under the real font and seeded into the scroller's size map, then the extent, the seek mapping and the end of the text are true before a chunk has rendered.

**Scope:** `TextChunker.ts` `measureChunks`, `averageCharWidth`; `TextMarquee.ts` `measureFont`, `seedChunkSizes`, `fontShorthand`, and the items watch that reseeds on rechunk.

**Renegotiable at:** Canvas text metrics — `measureText` is the

… [1,850 characters removed from the sample] …

 prose.

**Generates:** The marquee's `selection-join=" "`; the copy probe that reads two chunks as one line.

**Evidence:** `TextChunker.ts` `chunk`. Tests: "chunks join back to the source byte for byte, cut only at spaces, each keeping its trailing space", "a word longer than the target stays whole — the chunk extends to the next space".

**Impossible if true:** A chunk boundary inside a word. A chunk sequence that does not join back to its source.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/TextChunker.test.ts -t "byte for byte|stays whole"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

### The marquee composes the scroller and never extends it

**Invariant:** If the marquee needs the scroller, then it holds the scroller's exposed instance in a template ref and calls its public surface (`syncItemSize`, `updatePositionsImmediately`, `startAutoPlay`, `stopAutoPlay`, `visibleItems`, `selection`), and it never subclasses `VirtualScroller` or `HorizontalVirtualScroller`.

**Scope:** `TextMarquee.ts` (`scroller`, `play`, `pause`, `togglePlay`, `seedChunkSizes`); `TextMarquee.vue`.

**Mechanism:** The scroller stays pure (items, sizes, pixels); the marquee is composition. Extension would put words into the scroller's vocabulary and fork the tuned class for one consumer.

**Rejected alternatives:** A `TextScroller` subclass — the horizontal scroller would then carry chunking, fonts and a canvas.

**Evidence:** `TextMarquee.ts` header comment, `import { HorizontalVirtualScroller }` used as a type and a component only. Test: "play, pause and toggle delegate to the scroller’s autoplay through the exposed instance".

**Impossible if true:** `extends VirtualScroller.$Class` or `extends HorizontalVirtualScroller.$Class` in `TextMarquee.ts`.

**Verification:** `grep -n "extends" examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/TextMarquee.ts` prints nothing.

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

### Speed rides the creep integrator

**Invariant:** If the speed prop is px per second, then the marquee passes `1000 / max(1, pxPerSecond)` as the scroller's `creepMsPerPx`, so the glide is the scroller's own per-frame integrator and a slider change takes effect mid-glide with no restart.

**Scope:** `TextMarquee.ts` `creepMsPerPx`, `pxPerSecond`; the scroller's `creepMsPerPx` prop and `creepStep`.

**Mechanism:** The creep integrates speed × Δt per frame and reads the prop live every step, so the marquee never owns a timer or a frame loop of its own.

**Evidence:** `TextMarquee.ts` `creepMsPerPx`. Test: "px per second becomes the creep’s ms per px, floored at one px per second".

**Impossible if true:** A frame loop in `TextMarquee.ts`. A speed of zero producing a division by zero.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/TextMarquee.test.ts -t "ms per px"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

### The assumed chunk size never falls below the minimum

**Invariant:** If the scroller asks what to assume for an unmeasured chunk, then the answer is the target character count times the measured average character width, and never less than `minimumChunkWidth`.

**Scope:** `TextMarquee.ts` `assumedChunkSize`, `averageCharWidth`, `minimumChunkWidth`, `preMeasureCharWidth`.

**Mechanism:** Before the font is measured, the pre-measure average serves the first frame; a tiny target or a narrow font cannot push the assumption toward zero, which would collapse the extent and the seek mapping until seeds arrive.

**Evidence:** `TextMarquee.ts` `assumedChunkSize`. Test: "the assumed chunk size is the target times the average character width, never below the minimum".

**Impossible if true:** A chunk width the scroller assumes that is smaller than the minimum.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/TextMarquee.test.ts -t "never below the minimum"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-09-06

---
title: Testing & Invariants
description: 'A test is the invariant written for this implementation. How ivue classes are proven in three tiers, pure statics, hosted instances and browser probes, how each spec binds to a contract record the checker holds, and the protocol that keeps a check able to fail. The virtual scroller and its five companion classes are the worked example: nine colocated specs, sixty-three tests, two contracts.'
relatedPosts: [select-text-across-a-million-rows, templates-with-nothing-to-debug, single-file-models, agents-built-an-editor]
---

# Testing & Invariants

A test here is not a check that the code runs. It is the invariant, the
one if-then a piece of code exists to hold, written out for this
implementation so that it can fail. The class carries the behavior, the
contract carries the claim, the test binds the two, and a checker refuses
the repository when any one of the three is missing.

> A test is the invariant, written for this implementation.

This page is the method, with the virtual scroller and its five companion
classes as the worked example: nine colocated spec files, sixty-three
tests, two contracts, all read by the same checker that holds the engine's
own contract.

## Three tiers, by what the claim is about

Every claim about a class falls into one of three tiers, and the tier
decides what the test needs. The class layout makes the first cut for
you: a static has no instance `this` and cannot hold state, so it is
stateless by construction.

- **Pure statics.** A function of its arguments, no DOM. The range math
  of the selection, the speed ramp, the chunker, the pad's split and
  settle rules. The test calls the static through the namespace and
  asserts the return. Nothing is mounted, nothing is stubbed.
- **Hosted instances.** A class with cells, a constructor, and an owner.
  The scroller's window walk, the selection's drag, the touch gesture's
  hold, the marquee's seeding. The test constructs the instance with a
  plain object for its owner, stubs the two or three DOM readers the
  class rests on, and drives it by calling its methods.
- **Browser probes.** Claims about what the reader sees: a wheel lerp, a
  blank frame, a chip that appears. jsdom cannot see these. They run in a
  real browser through the component sweep, and the spec file names them
  as not covered.

The tier is a property of the claim, not of the file. One spec file
usually holds all three: statics at the top, hosted tests below, and a
line in its header saying which claims went to the browser.

## What ivue gives a test

The same rules that make a class readable make it testable, because both
come from the class declaring everything it does.

**Statics are reachable through the namespace.** The pure logic sits on
`X.Class` as static members, so a spec calls it with plain values and no
setup. The selection's range math is proven this way in seven cases that
never touch a node.

```ts
const Logic = VirtualScrollerSelection.Class;
expect(Logic.normalize(at(5, 3), at(2, 9))).toEqual({ start: at(2, 9), end: at(5, 3) });
```

**Cells are refs, derivations read live.** A ref-getter returns the same
cached ref every time, so a test writes `instance.speed.value = 50` and
reads the plain getter `instance.creepMsPerPx` on the next line. There is
no render to wait for, because a plain getter is a native getter.

**An owner interface is a plain object.** A hosted capability receives
what it needs through a small interface, never the host class. The
padding class needs four fields; the selection needs eight; the touch
gesture needs three methods and a flag. A spec builds that object with
`vi.fn()` where it wants to observe calls, and the capability cannot
tell the difference.

```ts
const owner = { halfPaddingQuantity: 3, scrollVelocity: 40, scrollGap: 800, estimatedItemSize: 40 };
const padding = new VirtualScrollerPadding.Class(owner);
expect(padding.pad(0)).toEqual({ before: 23, after: 18 });
```

**A subclass is the

… [6,000 characters removed from the sample] …

 a header line to a
record in a contract, a file named `<subsystem>.invariants.md` beside
the code. A record is one if-then with its scope, the mechanism that
makes it hold, the evidence, what is impossible if it holds, and a
copy-paste verification. The contract's generator section lists every
record as a gear and states the mechanism they form.

Code points back. An annotation at each enforcement point names the
record verbatim:

```ts
// invariant: The scroll position lands inside the scrollable range (examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/virtual-scroller.invariants.md)
if (!Number.isFinite(position)) return;
```

The checker reads all three homes and refuses drift in any direction: a
record no annotation references, an annotation whose record was renamed,
a header claim with no test, a test with no claim, a link whose anchor
does not resolve.

```sh
node .claude/skills/invariants/scripts/check_invariants.mjs --all --refs
```

The two contracts on this page are
[`virtual-scroller.invariants.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/virtual-scroller.invariants.md)
and
[`text-marquee.invariants.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/examples/playground/src/examples/text-marquee/text-marquee.invariants.md).
The first holds twenty-three records; five of them are reality-based,
the browser and the compositor deciding, and eighteen are chosen, the
subsystem's own disciplines standing on those five.

## The worked example

The padding class is the whole method in one short file: statics with a
permanent red arm, a hosted instance with an owner double, a fake clock,
and a header that binds every test to a record.

::: code-group
<<< ../../examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerPadding.test.ts [VirtualScrollerPadding.test.ts]
<<< ../../examples/playground/src/examples/virtual-scroller/VirtualScrollerPadding.ts [VirtualScrollerPadding.ts]
:::

The other eight spec files follow the same shape and sit beside their
classes:

| spec | tier | what it stubs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VirtualScroller.test.ts` | hosted | a Probe subclass pins the container size and exposes the seams |
| `HorizontalVirtualScroller.test.ts` | hosted | the same Probe over the subclass; asserts every seam names x |
| `VirtualScrollerItem.test.ts` | hosted | an element and a parent with two rect readers |
| `VirtualScrollerSelection.test.ts` | statics + instance | `elementFromPoint`, the caret API, rects; an owner object |
| `TouchSelectionGesture.test.ts` | instance | fake timers; touch events on real nodes, one detached |
| `VirtualScrollerPadding.test.ts` | statics + instance | an owner object; fake timers |
| `VirtualScrollerExample.test.ts` | instance | a static override to a thousand rows; a scroller object |
| `TextChunker.test.ts` | statics | the canvas context, once as null and once as arithmetic |
| `TextMarquee.test.ts` | hosted | a scroller object; the canvas context |

The visual claims run in the [component sweep](/examples/virtual-scroller):
the drag past the bottom edge, the touch long press and its chip, and
the flick that must never show canvas.

## The cost

A spec file is longer than a test file, because the header states what
the tests prove and the annotations repeat it above each one. That is
the price, and it is what lets a checker rather than a reviewer notice
that a claim lost its test. The other cost is discipline at the
boundary: a claim that grows a second dependent must move into the
contract, or the checker cannot see it.

A test is the invariant, written for this implementation.

## See it running

- [Virtual Scroller: 1M Items](/examples/virtual-scroller) — the class, its companions, and their specs as source tabs.
- [Text Marquee](/examples/text-marquee) — the chunker's specs, a pure Static class end to end.
- [The Invariants Behind ivue](/reference/invariants) — the engine's own contract, held by the same checker.

parts.text:
Done. Two commits on top of the padding work, nothing pushed.

**The double click** was the mousedown `preventDefault` taking the browser's multi-click units away along with the drag-selection. The selection class now handles a click count of two or more itself, selecting the word or the whole row as a settled range. The word unit treats punctuation as its own unit the way browsers do, which the sweep caught: the first version copied `divs,` and now copies `stacks`. Committed as `8e3da92b`.

**The testing method**, committed as `aa8f3217`:

- **Invar's protocol is already ours.** The `invariants` skill in this repo is byte-identical to Invar's, plus our own TypeScript checker on top, so there was nothing to port. What was missing was the application.
- **Nine colocated specs, 63 tests**, one beside each class of the scroller subsystem plus the marquee and chunker. Each opens with a generator header the checker binds to the sibling source, and every test carries the claim it proves. The specs had to move from `__tests__/*.vitest.spec.ts` to `X.test.ts` siblings because the checker resolves headers and tripwires only against that layout.
- **Two contracts** in Invar's record form beside the code: 23 records for the scroller, five of them reality-based, and 5 for the marquee. Source enforcement points carry the record annotations. The checker passes both and resolves 83 annotations and 79 generator links. Its 22 remaining problems all predate this work and sit in built `dist/` artifacts, the reference page's GitHub links, a newsletter test and the constitution's sibling rule.
- **Born red.** One defect planted per spec file, watched red, reverted. All nine went red on their plant.
- **The guide**, `guide/testing.md`, in the sidebar after Development & HMR with its OG banner: the three tiers, what ivue gives a test, the spec discipline as it applies to a class, the contract and checker, and the padding spec as the worked example. The two example pages gained source tabs for every spec and both contracts.

parts.text: did testing reveal more bugs?

Two real bugs and one wrong claim of mine.

- **Outside-press listeners leaked.** `clear()` removed the drag listeners but left the document-level mousedown and touchstart listeners armed, because it checked for a selection before it had nulled the range. Every cleared selection left two capture listeners on the document until the next drag. Found writing the selection spec, fixed in the double-click commit.
- **Double click copied punctuation.** The first word unit was any run of non-whitespace, so a double click on `divs,` took the comma. The browser sweep probe caught it, not the unit spec, which is the kind-match rule doing its job. Punctuation is now its own unit.
- **My prune claim was wrong, the code was right.** I wrote the repair spec as "measurements past the new end are dropped." The spec went red on correct code: the scroller drops only the run contiguous with the new end and parks farther keys so they resurrect if the list regrows. The claim was refined, not the code, and that caveat is now a record with a test.

Two things that look like bugs but are not. The chunker's per-font width cache leaked a stubbed measurement into a later spec, which is the class doing exactly what its record says, measure once per font. And the constitution test was failing at HEAD before any of this because its check counts were stale from the v-for alias check.

What testing did not find is also worth saying. The scroller's geometry, the clamp, the rebase, the spacers, the seek, the axis seams, the touch gesture and the padding all held on first write of their specs. Sixty-three claims, and the code disagreed with two.
Turn took 16s
do you feel tests strengthened the design and invariants did you run check programatically on them?

Yes on both, with one honest limit.

**Programmatic checks that ran.** The contract checker ran with `--all --refs` after every edit. Both contracts pass schema, and the run resolves 83 annotations and 79 generator links with zero problems in the touched files. That run holds the bijection in both directions: every header claim has an annotated test, every annotated test has a header claim, every `// invariant:` in source names a record that exists, every link anchor resolves. The specs themselves ran in the full suite, and each file was planted red once. What did not run is the `--score` fold and a `--depth verify` pass with independent re-derivation, and the checker cannot judge whether an annotation sits at a real enforcement point. That placement was by hand, at the guard each record's Mechanism names.

**Where the tests changed the design**, rather than only confirming it:

- The padding class's `settledVersion` became the one ref in the class with exactly one subscriber, the walk. That came from writing the settle spec and asking who would observe the bump. Before the spec, the re-walk was a vague "bump something."
- `selectAt` was extracted as a pointer-agnostic primitive for the double click, sitting beside `beginAt`, `extendTo` and `endDrag`. The touch gesture can use it later without a new seam.
- The listener code split into drag listeners and outside-press listeners, because the spec for `clear()` showed the two had different lifetimes and the old code had them fused, which was the leak.
- The demo's row count became a typed number instead of a literal type, so a test double can shrink it. Small, but it is the class admitting it has a knob.

**Where the invariants changed the tests.** Every `Impossible if true` line forced a negative test I would not have written from the positive claim alone: the NaN scroll position, the index outside the list, the anchor equal to the focus, a pad shrinking on the first decay frame, a chunk boundary inside a word. The owner interfaces held up under test pressure without a member added or removed, which is the strongest sign their sizes were right.

So the honest summary is that the code was mostly right, the specs found two defects and one wrong claim of mine, and the design moved in four small places toward what the specs needed, each a place where a lifetime or a subscriber had been implicit.
Turn took 25s

subtle bug in the vertical scroller both on dev and prod, there is subtle waviness that happens while scrolling it's hard to describe it's not constant but takes away from the smoothness we were reaching and previously seen in post player in realized repo for example

That is a real regression risk from the padding change, and I think I know the mechanism. During a wheel lerp the gap term shrinks every frame as the transform converges, so the trailing pad changes every frame, which means rows unmount at the top of the window on nearly every frame of the glide. Each mount and unmount forces a layout read from the item's size capture. Before the padding, the window only changed when the scroll crossed a row boundary. Measuring it before touching anything: window changes and DOM mutations per frame during a flick.

The one-pixel hop comes from the leading spacer being snapped to the device-pixel grid while the row transform underneath stays fractional, so rounding error changes each time the window's first row advances. I'll verify by measuring a row's on-screen position across a window change, then fix it by keeping the spacer fractional.

Found the bug: the leading spacer is being snapped like a landing, but it actually changes continuously during motion, causing sub-pixel jitter. Fixing it so only the transform snaps on seek landings while spacers stay fractional, then adding a spec test and re-measuring the hop.

The fix worked — both flicks now show zero hops, down from three and two, and the spec's expected count was off due to the fractional row shifting the window start. Next I'll check the staging-merge worktree of realized in case main is behind.

The fix carries over to the realized post player as the same one-line change, and all 273 tests pass cleanly. Now rebuilding the docs for the final sweep.

This looks like an intermittent jammed-main-thread issue since my isolated replay passed but the sweep failed—I'll loop the sweep's exact sequence with responsiveness checks and console capture to catch the failing iteration.

I've confirmed the double click fails when the target row is near the top of the frame (y≈16, 40px from viewport top) because the fixed nav bar intercepts the mousedown instead of the list, and the outside-press listener treats it as a click elsewhere, clearing the selection. I'll run one evaluate to confirm what element actually sits at that point.

Confirmed the pointer landed on the site's search button in the fixed nav bar, not the list—this is a probe issue, not a product bug, since the row picker fails to skip rows under the nav. I'll patch the picker and re-run the sweep.

parts.text:
Found and fixed, committed as `bb4351f6`, not pushed.

**The hop.** Your description was the key: smooth motion with an occasional one-pixel hop is a rounding seam, not a timing problem. The leading spacer was snapped to the device-pixel grid under the rule "motion is fractional, landings snap", but a spacer is not a landing. It changes at every window move, and the rows in the docs list are 111.375 px tall, so the spacer is a fractional sum. Rounding it while the transform under it stays fractional shifts everything visible by the rounding error each time the window advances. Following one row's on-screen position frame by frame against the transform showed the hops exactly on window-moved frames with integer spacers, up to 0.53 px. Both spacers now render fractional and only the transform snaps, only when a seek lands. Same probe after the change: zero hops.

**It was the same algorithm all along.** Not the padding, and not this session. The realized scroller in the staging-merge worktree, the newest one, snaps its leading spacer the same way with the same `snapForRender`, so the post player carries this hop too. The fix ports there as the same change: drop the snap on the spacer. Realized's main branch predates the snapping entirely, which is why it felt solid.

**What the probes could and could not see.** Frame timing, long frames and velocity dips were identical with the padding on or off and showed nothing. Position continuity of a tracked row saw it immediately. That is in LESSONS now.

**A separate finding in the sweep.** The flaky double-click cascade was the probe, not the product. When the page scrolls the frame to the top of the viewport, the site's fixed nav bar covers the first row, and a mousedown there lands on the search button. The row picker in the three vertical probes now skips anything under the nav bar. Sweep at 61 pass, 273 unit tests, gate clean, checker unchanged.
Turn took 13m 16s

Goal: harden the virtual scroller with specs, contracts and fixes. Everything is committed as bb4351f6 and green, including the sub-pixel hop fix and the double-click fix. Next: you push, then port the spacer unsnap to realized.

parts.text: Yes, i think you fixed it, it's now perfect :) <3

Good to hear, and that one was worth the chase.

The find that stays with me is how it hid. It was invisible to every metric that measures time, and obvious to the one that measures position. A hop is not a slow frame, it is a wrong number on a fast one. That is now a permanent probe in LESSONS, and the rule it enforces is in the contract with a spec arm behind it: spacers are fractional, only the transform snaps, only at a landing.

When you next touch the realized post player, the same one-line change removes the same hop there.
Turn took 5.2s
did we log it as test and invariant maybe?

Yes, all three homes, in the hop commit.

- **Test.** `VirtualScroller.test.ts` carries a new header claim, "If a row before the window has a fractional size, then the leading spacer renders that fraction unrounded; only a landing snaps," and the test under it measures one row at 30.375 px and asserts the spacer string keeps the `.375`. It fails against the old snapped spacer.
- **Invariant.** The record "The two spacers and the rendered rows sum to the extent" in `virtual-scroller.invariants.md` gained the mechanism sentence, the measured numbers, a rejected alternative naming the snap, and a new impossibility: a rendered spacer that differs from its size by a rounding.
- **Tripwire.** The `// invariant:` annotation now sits directly on `leadingSpacerPx` in the source, with a one-line comment saying why it is fractional, so the next person who reaches for a snap there reads the reason first.

The checker resolves all of it, and the probe method itself is in LESSONS. One gap I did not close: the hop probe is a scratchpad script, not a permanent sweep step. The unit arm guards the spacer value, but nothing in the sweep watches on-screen position continuity in a real browser. If you want that as a permanent instrument, it is a small addition to the sweep.
Turn took 7.8s
so it's gonna be more like a e2e test?

Yes, and it is the right tier for this claim. The unit test guards the number the class emits. Whether that number produces continuous motion on screen depends on the compositor and the real layout, which only a browser can answer. That is the kind-match rule: a visual claim needs a visual instrument.

The sweep already is that tier. It drives every docs component and playground route in a real Chromium with real input, and its selection probes are e2e in everything but name. The hop probe would be one more step there: flick the vertical list, follow one row's on-screen top against the transform for ninety frames, and fail on any frame where they disagree by more than a twentieth of a pixel. It runs in about two seconds and needs nothing the sweep does not already have.

Two things to decide on placement. The sweep runs on demand, not in CI, because it needs both built sites served locally, so the probe would guard releases and refactors rather than every commit. And the contract's Verification field for that record would then name both instruments: the vitest arm for the value, the sweep step for the motion. Say the word and I will add it, plus the Verification line.
Turn took 8.1s
add it to the sweep

The docs page shows 22 tiny 0.05-0.09px discrepancies that the playground doesn't have, and their pattern (largest at flick start, shrinking with speed) points to a scale factor between the row's rect and transform rather than a rounding issue—likely from a scaled/zoomed ancestor. I'll measure the ratio directly and check ancestors for transforms or zoom.

I found that the 22 reported "hops" are just sub-pixel autoplay creep (0.1-0.2 px per frame), not the real hops of 0.15-0.53 px seen on frames with significant motion. I'll tighten the probe to only judge frames with over 2 px of motion using a 0.1 px threshold, then re-run the sweep.
I'll tighten the threshold to 0.05 given the sub-0.03px noise floor, then reintroduce the old snap, rebuild, and confirm the probe fails red before reverting.

The rule confirmed a real hop, catching one at 0.06 px that the old 0.1 threshold would have missed. I've reverted the test change, rebuilt the source, and now I'll run a final sweep on the docs site with the checker.

The one-pixel shift looks like a separate issue from the whole-content hop I already fixed—likely a layout or raster phase change during the wheel lerp. I'll measure each mounted row's layout position across a wheel flick to determine which mechanism is causing it.

The pixel shift is a paint-time snapping issue, not layout drift — rows snap independently to the pixel grid and flip during fast fractional scrolling. Fix: snap transforms to whole pixels only above a certain speed threshold, and reset the sweep threshold back to 0.1. Now checking where the Lenis fork writes the transform to apply this.
Lens snap is in and gates are green, with all 53 scroller specs passing. Now running the continuity probe against the new transform and rebuilding the docs before the full sweep.

Committed as `e5b63311`, not pushed. Your dev server reads the source directly, so a reload shows it.

**The wheel shimmer** is a different defect from the hop, and the measurement said so before I touched anything: every mounted row's layout position stayed constant through a flick, so nothing moved in layout. What moves is paint. Rows sit at fractional layout tops, and when the compositor re-rasterizes the layer during a fast fractional glide, Chrome snaps each text line and box edge to the pixel grid on its own, so one row flips a pixel while its neighbour does not. The creep never re-rasterizes at its speed, which is why it stayed perfect.

**The fix is a split by speed** in the Lenis fork's transform write. At a device pixel per frame or faster, the transform lands on the grid, so the raster offset never changes and every row keeps its snap. Below that, the slow tail of a flick and the creep stay fractional, because snapping there turns the decay into irregular whole-pixel ticks, which is the chop the fork went fractional to avoid. Realized's old player rounded always and felt solid; the fork went fully fractional for the tail; the answer was both.

**The continuity step is now in the sweep**, and it earned its place the hard way. Its first threshold flagged creep-speed frames where the rect reports the sub-pixel transform quantized, which no reader sees, so it now judges only frames moving over two pixels at a tenth of a pixel. Planted with the old snapped spacer it went red at 0.46 and 0.25 px, reverted it went green, and it stays green with the speed snap. The contract's verification names both instruments, the unit arm for the value and the sweep step for the motion.

One honest limit. Rects cannot see the shimmer itself, only the hop. The speed snap is reasoned from the layout evidence and Chrome's raster behaviour, and your eyes on the wheel are the instrument that confirms it.

parts.text:
Yes, in a specific sense. Lenis writes whatever the lerp produces, a fractional number every frame, and leaves the browser to decide how that paints. Those three lines take that decision away from the browser and make it by speed, which is the one variable the compositor cannot know about.

What the fork now holds that stock Lenis does not:

- **The transform snaps by speed.** Fast motion on the device-pixel grid so the raster offset never changes and every row keeps its snap. Slow motion fractional so the compositor filters it into a glide instead of ticking.
- **Render-origin rebasing.** The transform and the leading spacer are shifted together by whole 65,536 px chunks so the rendered numbers stay under about 131k px, where single-precision compositing still resolves fractions. Stock Lenis stutters a million rows deep.
- **A virtual limit.** The wheel clamp comes from the computed extent, not the DOM, because the DOM never holds the content.
- **Fractional spacers.** Not Lenis's concern, but the other half of the same rule.

Each one is a place where the general library's answer was right for a page and wrong for a virtual list, and the receipt for each is a measurement rather than a preference. That is the honest framing: not more precise than Lenis in general, more precise about the one thing a virtual list at a million rows needs and a page never does.

The thing worth keeping is the rule itself, because it will come up again in the horizontal strip and anywhere else that composites long content: slow motion is fractional, fast motion and landings snap, spacers never snap.
