parts.text:
Committed as `c43cfed9`, not pushed. The first fix is verified here; the second and third need your iPhone.

**Edge zone, verified.** Autoscroll now starts 48 px inside each edge and ramps continuously through the edge and beyond, so a crawl near the edge, full speed past it, on both axes, for mouse and finger alike. The rule that only scrolled past the edge could never scroll a frame that is the whole page, which is the design flaw you named. A Chromium drive held the pointer 20 px inside the bottom edge and the list scrolled, the interior stopped it, the top zone scrolled back. Two specs cover it, one of them the page-sized frame case.

**Touch panning the canvas for real.** The frame is `overflow: auto` so Lenis can adopt native scroll, and it had no `touch-action`. On iOS, once our long press promotes, the first moves are cancelled by our `preventDefault`, but iOS stops honouring that as soon as it commits a pan, and then the frame's own `scrollTop` moves under the transformed rows, which is the text disappearing. The frame now excludes its own axis from native panning through a seam getter, `pan-x` on the vertical list and `pan-y` on the strip, so cross-axis swipes still reach the page. That also explains the horizontal strip on iPhone: the same native pan won the movement.

**The handles.** iOS shows native selection handles for any programmatic selection, so dragging them is the natural gesture there and it was extending a selection we did not track. Native selection changes inside the frame are now adopted as the logical range, so the chip's count and the copied text follow what you see. Our own re-pins are recognised by signature and ignored. Making the handles easier to grab is the part I have not touched yet, and it is yours to test first.

**What I could not verify.** Neither jsdom nor headless Chromium reproduces iOS Safari's pan commitment or its handles. The unit arms hold, the sweep is at 62 pass, and LESSONS records the three things iOS touch selection needs. Please try both lists on the phone: long press then drag, long press then drag the handles, and a drag toward the top and bottom edges.

If WebKit refuses to paint a native selection there, the CSS Custom Highlight API paints our range directly, with no native selection at all, which also removes the handles you found hard to grab. Committed as `b8eddc1c`, not pushed. Please try the phone again.

**What the engines said.** With WebKit running here, the in-zone touch hold scrolled the list and extended the selection correctly, and so did Chromium, at desktop and phone viewport sizes alike. That meant the selection logic was sound everywhere I could run it, and the phone was doing something the engines do not do headless.

**The cause.** Every frame of a drag re-pins the native selection with `setBaseAndExtent`. On iOS a native selection changing under a held finger hands the touch to the system's own selection handling: the page's touch is cancelled, our autoscroll loop dies with it, and the range freezes wherever the cancel landed. That is every symptom you described in one mechanism, including the painting that only caught up after release, while iOS held the gesture.

**The fix.** A finger's drag no longer touches the native selection. It paints the range through the CSS Custom Highlight API, which is pure paint and wakes nothing, and hands the finished range to the native selection only when the finger lifts, so the copy chip and iOS's own handles still work. Mouse drags keep the native selection throughout, since Ctrl+C reads it. The WebKit drive confirmed the shape: during the hold a CSS highlight and zero native ranges, after release one native range and a chip reading six rows.

**Where things stand.** Sweep at 62 pass, 57 scroller specs, gate clean, and the contract holds the new record with its impossibility, "a native selection call while a finger drags in a browser with the Highlight API". Two things I could not verify here and that only the phone can: that iOS no longer cancels the touch now that nothing selects under it, and that the painting keeps up as rows arrive.

That part is by design: the DOM shows the window, the data holds the selection, and the highlight re-pins as rows come back.

But your question exposes a real hole one step further on. After release the native selection is the clamped, mounted-only part of the range. If iOS then normalizes that selection even slightly, the signature no longer matches our own write, the adoption path treats it as the reader's, and it would shrink the logical range to the mounted rows, so the chip count would drop. The guard has to compare positions, not DOM nodes: a native selection that equals the logical range clamped to the window is our echo whatever nodes it sits on. Committed as `ec696ba4`, not pushed.

**The direct answer.** Native never needed to pick them up. The native selection has only ever covered the rows that are mounted, per frame with a mouse and on release with a finger, because a selection cannot span nodes that do not exist. The rows that vanished are held by the logical range, the chip copies from that range, and as rows come back into the window the highlight re-pins onto them. So a finger dragging through two hundred rows still copies two hundred rows.

**The hole your question found.** After release the native selection is the clamped, mounted-only slice. If iOS re-seats that selection on other nodes, which it does, the old echo guard compared DOM signatures, would no longer recognise our own write, and the adoption path would have taken the mounted slice as the reader's choice and shrunk the range to it. The chip would have dropped from two hundred rows to eighteen. The guard now compares positions: a native range equal to the logical range clamped to the window is our echo wherever its nodes sit. The spec plants exactly that case, a forty-row range pinned on five mounted rows and re-seated, and it stays forty.

**On your question, yes, honestly a real iOS Safari would change this loop.** What I have here is the WebKit engine Playwright ships, the same rendering engine as iOS Safari, and it has already settled two facts the phone alone could not tell me quickly. What it cannot do is the phone's touch handling: the long-press recogniser, the selection handles, the touch cancellation, the paint scheduling while a finger is down. Every remaining symptom lives exactly there, which is why each round costs you a test and me a guess.

What a macOS host would give me is the Simulator with Safari's Web Inspector attached to a real iOS WebKit, driven from the terminal with `xcrun simctl`, plus safaridriver for scripted touch. That is the instrument this class of bug wants, and it would turn the remaining items, blank rows, the vanishing scrollbar, the handles, into one session instead of a message per symptom. The cost is the environment move, and the on-device log is the cheap substitute in the meantime.

So the practical order: send me the log from one drag toward the bottom edge on the phone with `?touchdebug`, and I will read it now. If the `autoscrollStep` lines show `walk` advancing and `dom` growing with `text=0` on the last row, iOS is not painting the mounted rows while the finger holds, and the fix is a paint nudge. If `walk` does not advance, the window walk is not running under the touch, which is a scheduler problem with a different fix. Two commits, not pushed. Please push and test the phone.

**The paint nudge, `1472e4b3`.** The behaviour you described is one WebKit already has a name for in this codebase. Under an active touch it moves a promoted layer without rasterizing rows mounted during the move, and the Lenis fork's wheel path works around it by demoting and re-promoting the layer on every scroll write, with a layout read between. The selection's autoscroll writes the transform through the scroller instead and had no such step, so the rows past the fold mounted blank and the scrollbar thumb, a div in the same layer, went with them. The scroller now has `nudgePaint`, the same cycle, gated to WebKit because on Chrome the per-frame re-raster reads as shimmer, and the autoscroll asks for it after every write. A spec drives both the WebKit probe and the default, and the sweep is at 62 pass.

**The CI failure, `0c88bb43`.** Not our code. The repo has no root lockfile, so every GitHub install resolves fresh, and `vite-plugin-dts` 1.7 declares a caret range on `@microsoft/api-extractor` that now lands on 7.59.0, whose package exports remap the plugin's deep import to a path with a doubled `.js.js`. I reproduced it in a scratch install: 7.59.0 fails to load, 7.33.8 loads. The pin matches the version the shared node_modules already carries, so nothing changes locally and CI gets the working pair.

One honest note on the pin. It is a floor under an old plugin, not a cure. The durable fix is either a root lockfile, which the release conventions currently forbid, or moving `vite-plugin-dts` and `vite` forward together, which is a separate piece of work.

The two regressions came from my own last change, not the nudge. Skipping the selectability lock whenever a selection already exists means every second gesture, a long press on the selected text to extend it, or a press near the edge to keep going, hands the finger straight back to iOS's native selection, which is the exact failure we had fixed. On top of that, the new dismissal rule saw the lock hide the native selection and cleared the logical range under your finger. So two fixes: the lock is unconditional again, and a long press that lands inside an existing selection extends it from the far end instead of starting over, which gives touch its extension without depending on iOS's handles. A tap on the selection clears it, as iOS does.
